title: Canada Extends Remote Border Crossing Permit Deadline to December 2026
excerpt: The CBSA has pushed back the closure of its Remote Area Border Crossing program by nearly three months, giving 11,000 annual permit holders additional time to transition to a new telephone reporting system.
body:
• Canada has extended the deadline for its Remote Area Border Crossing (RABC) permit program from September 14 to December 1, 2026
  • Existing permits will now remain valid until November 30, 2026, giving travelers an additional 11 weeks
  • The RABC program will be permanently replaced by a telephone reporting system requiring all travelers to call CBSA upon entry
  • The program affects roughly 11,000 annual permit holders who cross the U.S.-Canada border at remote locations in northern Minnesota, Michigan, and Ontario

Canada's Border Services Agency (CBSA) has extended the deadline for its Remote Area Border Crossing permit program by nearly three months, pushing the closure from September 14 to December 1, 2026. The extension gives travelers additional time to adapt to a new telephone reporting system that will replace the decades-old permit program at remote crossings along the U.S.-Canada border.

What Changed

The RABC program has allowed eligible travelers — citizens and permanent residents of both countries — to cross into Canada at remote locations without physically presenting themselves at a port of entry. Under the updated timeline, existing permits will remain valid until 11:59 p.m. on November 30, 2026, an extension from the original September 13 expiration.

https://x.com/canadavisa_com/status/2088007634209362180

CBSA originally announced the program's closure on December 19, 2025, setting September 14 as the end date. The extension, reflected in updated CBSA guidance, provides additional transition time for the roughly 11,000 people who use RABC permits annually to operate small businesses, manage properties, and access fishing and recreation areas in remote border regions.

No new RABC applications are being accepted. Canada stopped issuing new permits in 2024 as part of a systematic review of the program.

The New System

After December 1, all travelers entering Canada through affected remote areas must report either in person at a port of entry or by telephone from a designated reporting site. The telephone reporting model requires travelers to call a CBSA number immediately upon entry with passport details, travel plans, and any required supporting documents. Travelers may still be directed to present in person if risk indicators arise.

The affected crossings span five remote areas: the Northwest Angle Area, the Pigeon River corridor through Lake of the Woods, the Canadian shore of Lake Superior, the upper lock system at Sault Ste. Marie, and Cockburn Island near Manitoulin Island.

"While I am disappointed that Canada has suspended a program that Americans and Canadians in border communities rely on, I am hopeful that its new remote access program will address the needs of these unique economies."

— Congressman Pete Stauber (R-MN), U.S. House of Representatives

Concerns Over Implementation

U.S. lawmakers, including Congressman Pete Stauber, Senator Kevin Cramer, and Congressman Jack Bergman, have formally written to the Canadian government expressing concerns about the transition. Local tourism operators, particularly resort owners in Minnesota's Northwest Angle who rely on Canadian fishing grounds, worry that poor cellular coverage in remote areas could make telephone reporting impractical and discourage visitors.

CBSA has said it is consulting with Indigenous communities, local governments, and law enforcement agencies to determine the placement of telephone reporting kiosks and signage. The agency maintains the new system will modernize border management, free frontline officers for higher-risk work, and align with procedures already used by U.S. Customs and Border Protection for remote-area crossings.

Impact on Cross-Border Indian Communities

The change carries particular significance for Indian immigrants and diaspora communities with ties on both sides of the U.S.-Canada border. Many Indian-Americans in northern border states maintain family, business, and property connections in Canada, while Indian-Canadians regularly cross into the U.S. The shift from a permit-based system to mandatory telephone reporting adds a layer of compliance that cross-border travelers will need to plan for, especially in areas with limited connectivity.

Indian nationals who are permanent residents of either country and currently hold RABC permits should note the extended November 30 deadline and familiarize themselves with the new reporting requirements before the transition takes effect.

What's Next

The location of new telephone reporting sites is expected to be finalized in the coming months. Travelers using remote crossings should confirm updated procedures through the CBSA website or by calling the Border Information Service at 1-800-461-9999. The extended deadline offers a window, but the program will not return after December 1 — marking the end of a system that has facilitated remote border crossings for decades.
